messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Does completeness imply the intersection property?
Completeness of (M,d) is assumed, and the sets F_n form a sequence of nonempty closed sets with F_{n+1} contained in F_n and diam F_n tending to zero.
Why is the sequence (x_n) Cauchy?
There is a selected point x_n in F_n for every n.
When m is greater than n, both x_m and x_n lie in F_n, so d(x_m,x_n) is at most diam F_n.
Since diam F_n tends to zero, the distances between x_m and x_n become arbitrarily small as m and n grow, and completeness gives a limit x in M.
Where does the limit x lie?
For an arbitrary N, each point x_n lies in F_N for every n at least N because of the nested condition.
The closedness of F_N then forces x into F_N, and the arbitrariness of N gives x in the nonempty intersection of all F_n.
Does the intersection property imply completeness?
The intersection property is assumed, and (x_n) is an arbitrary Cauchy sequence in M.
The sets F_k are defined as the closures of the sets of tail points x_n with n at least k.
Each F_k is nonempty and closed, and F_{k+1} is contained in F_k.
The Cauchy property of (x_n) forces diam F_k to tend to zero.
How does the intersection point relate to (x_n)?
The assumed property gives a point x in the intersection of all F_k, and for an arbitrary epsilon greater than zero we can choose k with diam F_k less than epsilon.
Does this complete the proof?
If n is at least k, both x_n and x lie in F_k, so d(x_n,x) is less than epsilon, which proves convergence to x and hence completeness of M.
